speaker: mikenadeau
text: Are you able to see the presentation? We are Mike. Okay, well, first off, Mr. Mayor and members of council, thank you very much for having us here this afternoon and this evening. There has been no greater pressure put on our organization aside from the homelessness file over the last few months or approximately a year. So we're really appreciate the opportunity just to come and update council on some of the work that we've been doing over the last few years. And then hopefully we'll have some questions at the end. So if it's okay, Mr. Mayor, do you want to just start the presentation? Absolutely, Mike, the floor is yours. Okay, so I thought I'd start with a bit of a background and I apologize for the slideshow karaoke in advance, however, I do think that I need to go through it verbatim. Social housing in Ontario is managed by 47 service managers as determined by the province. Northern Ontario is comprised of 11 service managers. There are 10 DSABs, District Social Services Administration Boards, and there's also the City of Greater Sudbury that is a service manager. Each DSAB is responsible for the service delivery over multiple municipalities or townships over thousands of square kilometers. So the 10 DSABs have a large geographic area. The City of Sudbury is only responsible for the city itself. All federal, provincial and municipal funding related to social housing is provided to the applicable service manager or DSAB. The Sault Ste. Marie DSAB supports or funds the following in the community. We fund 15 social housing providers. We are responsible to make sure that we have oversight over 2,221 social housing units. 26 new units were put in line this year alone. We are responsible for homelessness and homelessness prevention services and for food security. I just want to demonstrate that our 2020 budget to 2021 and 22 for housing services alone, in 2020 was $15.6 million. And this year our forecasted draft budget was $17.2 million. However, we do think it will be above that by the time some other provincial and federal grants come into play this calendar year alone. Of that $17.2 million for this year, 11.4 million is directly levied and paid for by the City of Sault Ste. Marie and Prince Township. So the vast majority of our housing division, which is one of four divisions for the DSAB, is funded through significant levy draw by the city. Homelessness and prevention. Service managers or DSABs are also responsible for homelessness and are mandated to have a 10-year housing and homelessness plan as set up by the province. Our plan includes the use of shelters, outreach workers, and a housing stability bank. Shelters offer a temporary bed and a safe place to stay for our homeless population. Outreach workers assist people staying in the shelters, people who are sleeping rough in the community, or members of the community in a social housing unit that come from the chronic homeless wait list. We also have the housing stability bank, and that bank provides funds, which is essentially a grant, for people who are behind in their rent and or their PUC as a strategy to prevent homelessness in the first place. Our shelter system. Shelters are open 24 hours a day, seven days a week. And our current system consists of 20 beds at Pauline's Place, and they serve women, youth, families, and people who have accessibility needs. We also have St. Vincent's Place, which has 14 beds. However, that was reduced to seven during COVID as a result of social distancing was not practical within their facilities. However, as Vincent's Place reduced its capacities, we added a temporary overflow shelter to better serve the community at the former Stilton Centre. We also use motels and hotels when required. If our shelter system is full, the shelters are full, we will not turn someone away who requires the bed for the night. We will put them up in a motel or a hotel if that was where they wish they desired. When someone enters our shelter, they are assessed using a triage approach, and the most acute people are eligible to be placed on our chronic housing wait list, and they receive high-intensity supports. It's also important to note that our DSEV was the first in Northern Ontario to develop a chronic housing wait list category in 2015-2016. People who are not placed on our chronic housing wait list are assisted to find accommodation and are offered light supports. We also have a housing prevention team, and approximately 25 people from multiple community agencies work together as part of that team to serve our marginalized community members. Since 2019, we have been making some significant strategic investments in our system. We recognize that our shelter system was weak, and when we compared it to peers, it was significantly underfunded. In 2019, we secured $900,000 from the province of Ontario to implement a low-income home ownership program, and that program is intended to allow people who do not have the down payment to be able to purchase a home that's renovated through Ontario Works, and then that program gets recycled through the DSEV on an annual basis. It's been working really, really well. We also purchased the Stilton Centre from the city of Sault Ste. Marie for $1, and allocated approximately $600,000 to renovate the space to operate as a shelter for a police place in 2020. We purchased the former Sacred Heart School to operate as a shelter, a transition house, transition rooms, and as a former NRC in 2020 at a cost of $500,000. We increased shelter wages to a minimum of $20 per hour in the better part of 2020 and later part of 2021. Before that, we had some shelter workers who were paid minimum wage, and when we looked at the turnover when we were speaking to our shelter partners, it only made sense that we made sure that they provide a decent competitive wage, so we updated it to have a mandatory minimum of $20 per hour per staff member. In 2020-2021, we also implemented the community wellness bus with our area partners, Surrey Hospital, CMHC, Algoma Family Services. We opened the COVID isolation shelter in 2021, and that is at capacity over the last few months. And we also leased and renovated the Verde Hall to operate as a temporary low barrier shelter, which will offer between 14 and 28 beds when it comes online. And the Verde shelter is a bridge until we get the former Sacred Heart renovated and operational, which is hopefully going to be in September of 2022. Some of our current plans include renovating eight transition units at the Stilton Centre at a cost of $355,000. Those are starting to open up. We already have three people who are residing there now, and the transition house are meant to be about a 30-day to a six-month stay until people can find permanent housing. So what we're looking at trying to do with our system is someone enters a shelter, they go to transition housing, and then they go into more permanent housing over time. We are currently renovating the former Sacred Heart school to operate as a shelter, and it will have a minimum of 14 shelter beds and also a minimum of 22 transition units, and it will also include the NRC. And Dr. McLean has agreed to provide services out of the NRC. Our community partners are going to be providing service, so we're really excited to get that back up and running. The cost when we finally complete renovating Sacred Heart will be in the millions of dollars. There'll be many millions of dollars that we're spending on that. I do not want to state the budget just because we will be issuing a tender, and we're trying to make sure that our costs are as low as possible. We've also purchased a new asset that will be renovated and allow us to accommodate a minimum of additional 14 affordable housing units over the next three months, we hope, in 2022. So by 2022, we will have added 44 new affordable units into the community mix. Our homelessness-related budget. As I stated, we've made some significant investments since 2019. However, COVID was also a factor and has been a significant increase in provincial and federal funding. In 2019, we were spending a little over $2 million on homelessness-related funding. In 2020, it was 3.8 million. In 2022, it's a little over 5 million. And in 2022, our budget will be approximately $4 million is what we're going to be spending on the homelessness file. We also completed our third pit count, which was held on the week of October 25th. And our pit count is a point-in-time count where we go out for the week and we complete a count of all the homeless people that we can find across the community in order to accurately gauge and assess how we're doing and just how many community members need our help. This year, for the first time, we expanded the scope of our homelessness count and we included the hidden homelessness, i.e. the couch surfing, and that provided a dramatic increase to our numbers. Last time we did a pit count, we tried to do them every two years. We did one in 2016, which was 74 people we found. 2018, we uncovered 93 individuals. In 2021, we had to wait three years because of COVID. We counted 244 people that were classified as homeless within the community. That's an increase of 151 people, which is significant, but we'll get into a little bit of the data to show why. Some of the makeup that we wanted to highlight, in 2018, 28% of the homeless population were female. In 2021, that has jumped up to 40%. So it is a significant increase in the population and Pauline's Place is doing a marvelous job in providing service to those individuals. Another thing that we would like to highlight, in 2018, 37.5% of the individuals we counted self-identified as indigenous. This year, that population that has self-identified, 65% of our community, of the homeless community has self-identified as an indigenous person. That's really important data to understand. The last census data that we had, 12% of the community self-identified as indigenous. However, 65% of our homeless population self-identified. So we do know that we have a significant over-representation of the population. We also wanted to show some of our shelter nights. The shelter usage is going up dramatically. In 2020, Pauline's Place had 2,027 visits. As of the end of October, which we still had another two months to go, they were at 3,338 nights. In St. Vincent Place had 2,852. When we counted St. Vincent's and the overflow shelter combined for the men, we're up to 4,021 room nights for the year to date. There is a significant need for additional supportive housing in the community. Currently, right now, we have 10 units that are operated 24-7. We have an additional 13 units that provide semi-supports for eight hours a day. There is a need for, based on the last pit count, there's a need for up to 60 additional supportive housing units to be added into the community. And when we talk about supportive housing, what we're talking about is people need supports for their health. They also need supports with mental health and addictions. They may need to take medication, harm reduction services, cultural services, meals, and room cleaning. Supportive housing is something that this community has been trying to get for many, many years, and it's just starting to get more acute. Supportive housing requires three items at a cost of approximately $50,000 per year per room. So first, we need a new capital investment to purchase or build a new facility, a new apartment building. The DSEP can provide that. We have access to private market lending, and we can handle a capital investment of significant, significant value. Then the rents also need to be subsidized because people, if you're in receipt of Ontario Works, your rent is only $397. Your shelter allowance is only $397 a month, and we know that rent, just on a break-even point, is much more than that. But the DSEP can assist with rent subsidy. The third leg of the stool that we require to make it balanced requires a new investment from Ontario and or Canada. Supportive housing complex requires approximately $3 million in annual new funding over a 20-year period, or a $60 million total investment. So it's the supports that we require in order to make this strategy work. We know that we can provide new housing. We know that we can put people in apartments. However, our experience has clearly demonstrated that without that health support and 24-7 supports to people residing independently, their tenancy will not be successful. Rooms get damaged. There will become issues with neighbours, et cetera, et cetera. And if a tenant is evicted from social housing, and for example, they may have a $30,000 damage to their room or to their apartment whenever it gets renovated, they can never get back into social housing until that debt is cleared within the province of Ontario. So really, it's setting the person up for failure if we do not have the proper supports available to the person to make sure that tenancy is successful. Mr. Mayor, that concludes my brief overview of our system, and I'm sure that there are some questions from either yourself or members of council that we'd be happy to entertain.
